item.title: Drive-Away Dolls, 2024 - ★★★
item.description:
has all the stuff i generally appreciate in a coen comedy joint; everyone seems to be simultaneously bewildered and incredibly suave, there are some fucking absurdly stupidly funny visual gags (the ribbon tied around the dildo? cmon now), and does it make sense if i say that the camerawork is super witty? i take umbrage, though, with almost everything else. Qualley and Viswanatha certainly give it a go, but it just does not seem to work out for either of them. i get what Qualley is going for with the Clooney-in-O-Brother-Where-art-Thou schtick, but she totally fumbles the landing in my eyes. and Viswanatha's awkward lesbian routine is just a litttttle too awkward for my liking.

also: can we talk about some of those scene transitions in the first half? they were too much, weren't they? i think we can all agree that they were too much.

also also: we can add this one to the list of films where Matt Damon doesn't turn up the third act (Interstellar, Saving Ryan's Privates, etc.). Like, I know he shows up on a billboard about halfway through, but that isn't his true Form. in fact, that makes me think: what would be the Platonic Ideal of Damon? it's probably just the "how do you like them apples" scene in Good Will Hunting, right?

anyway. probably constitutes the bare minimum for 'enjoyable movie.' hope the coen bros get back together soon

item.title: Mysterious Skin, 2004 - ★★★★½
item.description:
one of the greatest queer films, maybe the greatest, but what holds me back from the 5 stars that i'd so love to give it is that i'm not entirely sure i'm won over by the alien abduction vein; i understand that it's there for a reason — and i admit that it's powerful, especially in retrospect, and especially that first UFO scene — but there's maybe a loose linkage in the chain that binds these two stories together, and that results in what verges on non-sequitur at points. then again, cohesion maybe isn't what this is going for at all, and i respect that. still, i felt that there was something missing. but the better a film is the more picky i have to be. gordon-levitt is fucking electric here, such a profound performance that it's difficult to put it into words. and the ineffable ecstasy and agony of queer life had never before been put to film quite like this, and it hasn't been since. it sidesteps the kind of staleness that i feel so many queer coming-of-age films amass by being just so goddamn honest. there's a lot of fucking truth in this. and sometimes truth is excruciating. 

i reckon a second viewing would do it good vis-a-vis its rating, but unfortunately it's the type of film which takes a long time to give a second chance, for obvious reasons. not because i'm traumatised or so upset by its contents that i can't bear to rewatch or anything; more so because i feel like i wouldn't be giving it due respect if i were to watch it again without waiting a while. i reckon its slightly base to watch something like this repeatedly.

item.title: Sometimes I Think About Dying, 2023 - ★★★★
item.description:
small movies about big things like this. this thing suits the form of cinema so well - reminds me of Kitty Green's The Assistant in a lot of ways, also some quite Terrence Malick-esque editing - that i can't quite imagine how it can possibly be based on a stage play.

plays with cinematic language with such tactful intelligence; feels intimate, but also gives itself air to breath: show-not-tell to the nines. it knows that its audience can pick up what it puts down with relative ease, but it never slips into obviousness or triteness. 

and the sort of emotional movements in terms of audience response are very nicely moderated. perspectives shift with a line or two, and it's all quite controlled. cinematography elegant, direction to-the-point but provocative, performances: some of the best i've seen all year. Daisy Ridley is great, but the stand-out is obviously Marcia DeBonis, who sneaks right up on you. likewise, the film is pretty unassuming at first, but by the end it's like a tear's been hanging on to your chin for a while and it finally lets go

item.title: I Saw the TV Glow, 2024 - ★★★★½
item.description:
Jane Schoenbrun’s 2021 We’re All Going to the World’s Fair was the best film about the internet since 2002’s Demonlover, and it perhaps even surpassed Olivier Assayas’ glossy neo-noir in its understanding of the internet as an autonomous, malevolent being. The internet of Demonlover is inert, a towering black monolith to be infiltrated; its characters move into the internet, they explore its dark corners as they might any other shady organisation or corporation — in short, it’s a crime scene to be investigated. But in World’s Fair the internet is a monstrous, inescapable shadow, one which haunts and infects the mind. Schoenbrun’s film is incredibly sensitive to the dissociative and oftentimes dysphoric kind of relationships (with others and with ourselves) that something as unforgivingly heterogeneous as the internet can facilitate, especially for the lonely. The internet through Schoenbrun’s lens is active: a creature with limbs, which preys on its users, and can reach into the physical world and drag them into its grimy trenches, where identity seems to dissipate into pixels.

World’s Fair and Demonlover were written almost two decades apart, and their disparate representations of the internet and internet culture could easily be explained away by the development of the internet itself over those twenty years — the internet we see in Demonlover evolved, so to speak, into the internet we see in World’s Fair. This is true, of course, the internet does seem frighteningly proficient in adapting to its surroundings, and of reflecting the ethos of the society it serves from year to year (even day to day), and certainly the internet of twenty years ago was not so capable of engendering the identity crises in which World’s Fair is so interested. But other things were. Schoenbrun’s newest film, I Saw the TV Glow, exposes even more beautifully (and at points even more nauseatingly) the same ineffable feelings of discordant identity that the director touched on so intimately in World’s Fair, and yet the internet is entirely uninvolved. It’s set in the nineties, and it’s not about creepypastas, or ARGs, or /x/ forums, or some other internet mode of storytelling only really fathomable to post-9/11 teens. It’s about television.

Schoenbrun’s concern in World’s Fair, then, was not the internet itself (or at least not just the internet itself), but the internet as a reflector of the parasitic, dissociative relationship that we have and have always had with the media that we obsess over. I Saw the TV Glow is the proof to back up that idea: it notes our propensity for morphing to fit the content we consume, it considers the fallout which that sort of violent self-fashioning leaves in its wake years down the line, and it asks if the content that we consume consumes us just as much in return. But the film also orbits around an enigmatic but brazenly self-assured trans metaphor, currents of which were present in World’s Fair, but which in I Saw the TV Glow blooms into one of the most staggeringly nuanced expressions of queer experience in recent memory.

item.title: Challengers, 2024 - ★★★★½
item.description:
If for some reason you thought that Luca Guadagnino couldn’t make tennis sexy, you can keep thinking. Over the past fifteen years, the Italian auteur has managed to make almost everything he touches brim with carnality — the aristocracy, David Hockney, age gaps, satanic dance rituals, cannibalism; Guadagnino makes the repellant, the mundane, and the uncanny as seductive as the Lady in Red. And in his newest film, Challengers, a steamy sports drama just as preoccupied with the power-play of love as its characters are with getting into Zendaya’s pants, he makes tennis — a sport that Guadagnino himself considers mind-numbingly boring — so fucking sexy that, in comparison, sex seems about as sexy as, well, tennis.

In the world of Challengers, a sentence as innocuous as “look at that backhand” becomes a statement of intense physical attraction: as soon as Art Donaldson (Mike Faist), a rising junior tennis champ, utters those words, he inadvertently sets into motion a back and forth rally that will last years. He’s talking about Tashi Duncan (Zendaya), who is about to absolutely crush her poor, unassuming opponent — when she does, she lets out an unforgettable scream of total domination. Soon enough, Art will find himself subject to that same energy, but for now her outburst is as enticing as anything he’s ever seen.

The same can be said for his childhood best friend and doubles partner Patrick Zweig (a ratty Josh O’Connor), who, unsurprisingly, is equally infatuated with Tashi. Cut to a sweaty midnight tryst in Patrick and Art’s shared hotel room — set to the hot and lavish music of Blood Orange, a favourite of Guadagnino’s — a meeting which culminates in one of the single most hilariously tantalising shots in recent memory, and the infatuation cements itself as one for the ages.

item.title: Dune: Part Two, 2024 - ★★★★½
item.description:
It was only in the ten or so years before the release of Star Wars in 1977 that truly great, artistic features began to make a shit-load of money (think The Godfather, Rocky, Jaws, The Exorcist), and A New Hope made more money than anything that had ever come before it. Thus, behind the glamour and the spectacle of George Lucas’ era-defining space-western, some executives saw that a massive business opportunity was materialising — forty-six years later and the Star Wars brand now comprises eleven films, with a touted twelve more on the way, fourteen TV shows with twenty-five seasons between them, over a hundred novels, over a hundred video games, over a thousand comic books, several theme park attractions, and an entire religion.

The more twitter-savvy (sorry, X-savvy) among you may have seen that Christopher Nolan recently compared Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Two to The Empire Strikes Back. High praise, sure, but there’s something slightly disconcerting in that comparison. When audiences saw Denis Villeneuve’s Dune in 2021, they were treated to a taste of what it might have been like to see Star Wars in May of 1977 — it wasn’t much like anything they had seen before, and a breath of fresh air between all the Star Wars, the MCU, the Mission Impossible, the Fast and Furious; all the franchises which had dominated the box office for the previous decade. Here was a novel, exceptional piece of science-fiction that was genuinely exciting and engaging, and that wasn’t reliant on having seen thirty other films and five TV shows to fully understand it. And it made a lot of money. 

The success of Dune: Part One harboured a fear, only exacerbated by the many Star Wars comparisons that it provoked, that Hollywood would wildly misunderstand the reason behind its success — Dune: Part One made as much money as it did because it of its brilliance, its focus, its beauty, not because of its IP. There was a danger that Part One only marked the beginning of a never-ending bombardment of branded content, that Dune would gradually regress into a soulless corporate entity long past its artistic peak, and that a sequel would be the first step into that regression. Thankfully, Dune: Part Two makes it glaringly evident that Villeneuve has no intention of letting that happen.

item.title: Arrival, 2016 - ★★★★½
item.description:
its so refreshing sometimes just to engage with something truly smart, that doesn't look down on its audience, doesn't elevate itself above what it is, knows how to be itself, can elicit emotion to a level beyond expectation.

in a world saturated by short-form, meaningless content, which preys and capitalises on our every second of attention, which reduces art to nothing - films like arrival are completely necessary. it's a rebuttal against "turn-your-brain-off" content. it's stimulating, but not in the least part exhausting - it's invigorating. "turning your brain on" does not require mental work. it just stops you slipping into complicity. 

great film, always a great time; cried; texted my mum (it was too late at night to call).
